HINDUISM - THE WAY OF KARMA AND SAMSARA - STUDY NOTES

A HINDU VOICE (NAREN)
- Naren: being a Hindu is central to his life; he tries to live well in the cycle of lives that works out his destiny.
- Practising his faith is 'a very tactile experience which affects all my senses' - sounds, smells, colour, movement, dance and ritual.
- This world shapes his character for the next life on the cycle of Samsara.

ORIGINS
- Hinduism is one of the oldest living religions.
- Roots go back to 2,500 BCE, to the Vedic religions of people living along the banks of the Indus river in India.
- Archaeological evidence shows worship of many gods and the practice of meditation.
- From Vedic worship of nature-gods came the ideas of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver) and Shiva (destroyer).
- Trimurti: the three aspects or faces of the Supreme God, Brahman - Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.

WHERE HINDUS LIVE
- Main religion in India, Nepal and Bali.
- Also in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa and the West Indies.
- Many Hindu emigrants settled in Europe and North America in the mid 1950s.
- 910 million Hindus worldwide; about 300,000 in Britain.

NATURE OF HINDUISM
- No founder and no prophets.
- No particular church (ecclesiastical) or institutional structure, and no set creed.
- Emphasis on a way of living rather than a way of thinking.
- Radhakrishnan, a former President of India: 'Hinduism is more a culture than a creed.'
- Its origins cannot be traced to any historical person; open to different views, which has led to huge diversity.
- Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism emerged from Hinduism.
- A complex tapestry: mystical thought and ascetic practice exist alongside animal worship and magic. A Hindu can be polytheist, monotheist, pantheist or have another form of devotion.

WHAT DO HINDUS BELIEVE?
- No central teaching authority.
- Vedas: the sacred Hindu writings; they guide Hindu thought and life but have many, often conflicting, interpretations.
- Many gods (devas) and goddesses (devis): different ways of experiencing and understanding the supreme God, Brahman, who can never be fully known.
- Brahman: the Supreme God / ultimate Supreme Being to which all gods lead.
- Vishnu: the most popular incarnation of Brahman. He and his wife Lakshmi have come on earth many times to strengthen people's faith.
- Avatars: human embodiments or incarnations. Vishnu has had nine, notably Krishna (eighth) and Buddha (ninth); one final avatar is yet to come.
- Some Hindus believe in many gods (for weddings, birthdays, festivals, morning and evening); others believe in only three, the Trimurti. All believe in one ultimate Supreme Being.
- You must worship God, but the most important thing is how you live.
- Dharma: doing what is right and correct for you; moral and religious duty; 'right conduct'.
- Karma: the law of cause and effect - do good and good happens to you; do bad and bad happens.
- Karma is not necessarily fatalistic: by judgement and forethought it can be used to good advantage.

VISION OF SALVATION
- A person is reborn (reincarnated) until they become perfect - many existences.
- Atman: the soul or inner self; after death it moves to a new body.
- Samsara: the endless cycle of rebirths.
- Hindus live good lives so each rebirth brings them closer to moksha.
- Moksha: complete union and peace with God; liberation from the cycle of rebirth and from the limits of ignorance.
- The liberated soul rests in peace: in blissful isolation, by absorption into Brahman, or by communion with a personal god.
- Gurus: spiritual teachers who show how to reach moksha. Believers visit them in an ashram (retreat or hermitage).
- Sadhus and Sannyasins: ascetics or hermits who renounce earthly pleasures and devote their lives to God - one way to salvation.

THE FOUR ASHRAMAS (STAGES OF LIFE)
- Each stage has its own social and religious duties and needs virtues (dharma) such as compassion, gentleness, modesty and forgiveness, as in the Bhagavad Gita.
- 1. Student: work hard, obedience and respect, disciplined life.
- 2. Householder: follow a career, take responsibility for home and family.
- 3. Retired: detachment from family concerns; study the sacred texts.
- 4. Ascetic (optional): a man may leave his family and become a wandering holy man.
- The ashramas do not apply to Shudras or women. Most men stay in stage two; the last two are honoured more in spirit than in practice.
- Aims of following dharma: Kama (pleasure, enjoyment of life); Artha (wealth, material comfort); Moksha (release).
- Spiritual perfection: when atman is at one with the universal Brahman.
- Following dharma builds good karma, giving a better rebirth on samsara.
- Varnashramadharma: Hindu guidelines for life (varna + ashrama + dharma).

THE CASTE SYSTEM
- Caste system: an ancient social-class system where people are born into groups (castes), each with its own rules and traditions.
- Originally all classes were seen as equal; slowly they came to be fixed by birth rather than personal qualities.
- Origin in the Rig-Veda creation story: when Brahman's body was divided, 'his mouth became the priests; his arms, the soldiers; his thighs, the merchants; his feet, the servants'.
- Four varnas: Brahmins - teachers and priests (head); Kshatriyas - rulers and warriors (arms); Vaishyas - farmers and merchants (thighs); Shudras - labourers and servants (feet).
- Untouchables (Harijans): a separate non-caste group doing the lowliest, dirtiest jobs, e.g. working with leather (the cow is sacred).
- Jobs no longer decide caste (a Brahmin can be a cab driver, a Kshatriya an accountant), but endogamy (marriage within the group) is the norm.
- You can move caste when reborn if you lived a good previous life.
- Penalties for mixing castes: ritual cleansing or paying for a feast for your own caste.
- Louis Fischer, The Life of Mahatma Gandhi: 'Untouchability is segregation gone mad.' Gandhi fought it for the sake of the castes and the outcasts, defying 'a thousand taboos'.
- Gandhi admitted untouchable families into his ashram and his home, to the distress of his family and community.

THE COMMUNITY OF BELIEVERS - SCRIPTURES
- Hinduism is not a single unified religion but a system of varied beliefs and rituals within Hindu society.
- Scriptures written in Sanskrit, the ancient language of India and root of modern Indian languages.
- Shruti ('hearing'): 'heard' from the gods; eternal, sacred, cannot be changed.
- The four Vedas: Rig-Veda (Book of Hymns); Yajur-Veda (Book of Religious Ritual); Sama-Veda (Book of Chants and Worship); Atharva-Veda (Book of Charms and Spells).
- Upanishads ('sit down near your teacher'): later dialogues between students and gurus exploring the Vedas; teach that Brahman is present everywhere and in all living things.
- Smriti ('memory'): traditions passed down generations; explain practically how to live the Shruti in laws and codes of conduct.
- Smriti includes the great epics Mahabharata and Ramayana, with heroes such as Rama, Sita and Krishna.
- Much authority lies in Smriti and the community; the caste system's influence is strongest here.
- Common observances: ritual purification (external - washing, bathing; internal - yogic exercises), devotional practices (private and communal), pilgrimage and festival.
- Each person finds their own path according to ability and personality. The tension between personal path and community custom is where faith grows.

A CELEBRATING TRADITION - WORSHIP (PUJA)
- Most Hindus worship one manifestation of God (e.g. Vishnu or Shiva) at a shrine; temples are dedicated to particular gods.
- Puja: worship. Begins at dawn, repeated at noon and evening.
- Gayatri mantra: the most common Hindu prayer: 'Om. Let us think about God who made the world, may He guide our minds.' From the Rig-Veda (3.62.10), 'mother of the Vedas'. Used in all prayers of caste Hindus, as grace before meals, and repeated hundreds of times in meditation.
- Om (Aum): sacred syllable, a mystic salutation meaning 'hail'. Said before any prayer, at the start and end of Vedas readings, written at the top of a page or exam paper. Upanishad: 'It is with Om that one begins to sing.'
- Puja ritual: shoes removed; women cover heads with saris; bell rung to start; image dressed and garlanded with flowers; food offered; scripture chanted; devotee moves clockwise around the shrine (as the earth moves around the sun); water for purity; incense; sacred fire or lamp.
- Worship is usually individual or in small groups; congregational only at festivals. Temple worship is not required.
- The image is treated as a royal guest. Priests and devout people wear forehead marks.
- In large temples only the priest (Brahmin) enters the shrine and makes offerings (usually flowers and fruit). Cost does not matter if given with love. The priest may burn part and smear ashes on the forehead.
- Kalasha: a clay or copper pot of water closed with leaves and a coconut. Pot = human body, water = soul (water of life). Used to honour Naruna, lord of water. Placed on the highest part of the shrine, carried on the head; water (from a sacred river) sprinkled for purification and protection.

HINDU FESTIVALS
- Occasions of music, dance, stories, shared food; break routine and raise new hope.
- Lunar calendar - some festivals dated by phases of the moon.
- Rama: seventh avatar of Vishnu; adventures of Rama and wife Sita feature in several festivals.
- Desara (Sept/Oct): story of Rama's search for his kidnapped wife; triumph of good over evil; effigies of Ravana, king of demons, are burned.
- Divali ('row of lights'): autumn, five days; recalls Rama and Sita's return from exile. Lamps, fireworks, gifts, prayers to Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity. New Year on day four - forgiving, forgetting, good wishes. Light = victory of goodness. Lakshmi visits every home with a row of lights.
- David Harmer's poem 'Divali': winter 'stalks us like a leopard'; 'I will light my lamp for you Lakshmi, drive away the darkness'.
- Holi: festival of fertility, three days; street dancing, bonfires, coloured powder and red-stained water (new blood in veins). Worship of Krishna and his consort Radha; hymns; Arti ('services of light'); prasad (sacred food) shared.
- Kumbha Mela: every twelve years, millions bathe where the Ganges and Yamuna meet. Rivers symbolise life without end. Majjana (immersion) purifies body and soul.
- Sodhana: bathing as cleansing; snana: spiritual purification. The Ganges is the holiest river; its bathing steps are ghatas.
- Ganesha: elephant-headed god, son of Shiva, one of the best loved.
- Varanasi (Benares): most holy pilgrimage city, linked with Shiva.

RITES OF PASSAGE
- Birth: father writes 'Aum' on the baby's tongue with a gold pen dipped in honey - hope the child speaks truth, sweet like honey. Later first hair cut - badness from a previous life will not affect the new life.
- Adolescence: Sacred Thread ceremony (Upanayana) - spiritual initiation of boys. Thread placed from shoulder to waist before a sacred flame; mantras, gifts. He can then perform puja and is called 'twice born'.
- Marriage: arranged marriages are the norm. Three sets of rules: Law of the Land; Customary Law (local practice); Brahmanical Law (scriptures). Held in bride's home; red sari, jewellery, saffron-dyed hands and feet; garlands, special swing. Ceremony around a sacred fire (symbol of the sun); the god Agni witnesses the marriage. Seven steps around the fire: food, wealth, strength, children, good luck, happiness, friendship. Guests pass hands through flame and touch forehead (cleansing). Lasts two to three days. Necklace of black beads and two gold semi-circles - unites two families.
- Death: body wrapped in white (male) or red (female), carried to a funeral pyre for cremation. Closest male relative lights the fire. About twelve days later food offered in thanksgiving. Ashes scattered into a river after three days.
- Sanatana Dharma: 'eternal order' - governs all life.

CHALLENGES TO THE TRADITION
- Millions practise as for centuries; others (mostly in the West) combine practice with modern life - weekly temple visits, mantras and meditation at a home shrine.
- Hundreds of sacred occasions involve fasting, bathing, chanting and gifts.
- Outlawed but hard to abolish: child marriages, sati/suttee (burning a widow beside her dead husband), treatment of Untouchables.
- Inter-faith: Hindu-Muslim relations (11th-18th centuries) ranged from persecution to attempts to fuse both faiths, e.g. under Akbar (1556-1605).
- Christianity arrived with the Portuguese in the sixteenth century.
- Influenced by Christian ideals: Sri Ramakrishna (1836-86), founder of the Ramakrishna movement; Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941), Bengali poet; Mahatma Gandhi (1869-1948), passive resistance to British rule (satyagraha).
- The general population is unaffected by Christian missions; increasing resistance to conversion.
- Common links with other faiths: a Divine Power as source of life; praising the Divine Power; the Golden Rule; consequences of good and bad actions; teachings on suffering and death.
- Others named: Vinobha Bhave; Vivekananda (Hindu monk, 1863-1902).
- Gandhi: 'The cow is a type for all that lives.' Louis Fischer: 'Gandhi was too great to succeed.'
- Yoga: a spiritual discipline with ethical demands; commercialising it for fitness loses its essence.
- Bhagavad Gita, Krishna: 'As a man leaves an old garment and puts on a new one, so the spirit leaves his mortal body and puts on one that is new' and 'You shall reap what you sow'.

KEY TERMS
- Vedas, Brahman, Vishnu, Avatars, Krishna, Brahma, Shiva, Dharma, Karma, Atman, Samsara, Moksha, Ashramas, Caste system, Shruti, Smriti.

rows.prompt: Explain the terms dharma and karma.
rows.model_answer: Dharma is doing what is right and correct for you - your moral and religious duty or right conduct. Karma is the law of cause and effect: if you do good, good will happen to you; if you do bad, bad will happen. Following your dharma well builds up good karma, leading to a better rebirth.

rows.prompt: Outline briefly the Hindu vision of salvation.
rows.model_answer: Hindus believe the soul (atman) is reborn many times in the cycle of samsara until it becomes perfect. By living good lives they move closer to moksha, liberation from rebirth and ignorance, and complete union and peace with God. The liberated soul rests in blissful isolation, is absorbed into Brahman, or lives in communion with a personal god.

rows.prompt: Name and describe the four ashramas.
rows.model_answer: Student: work hard, obey and lead a disciplined life. Householder: follow a career and look after home and family. Retired: detach from family concerns and study the sacred texts. Ascetic (optional): leave family to become a wandering holy man devoted to religion.

rows.prompt: Name the four varnas of the caste system and their roles.
rows.model_answer: Brahmins are teachers and priests (the head). Kshatriyas are rulers and warriors (the arms). Vaishyas are farmers and merchants (the thighs). Shudras are labourers and servants (the feet). The Untouchables, or Harijans, are a separate non-caste group.

rows.prompt: Explain the words Shruti and Smriti, giving an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Shruti means 'hearing': scriptures heard from the gods, eternal and unchangeable, such as the four Vedas and the Upanishads. Smriti means 'memory': traditions passed down that explain how to live the Shruti in laws and codes of conduct, such as the epics Mahabharata and Ramayana.

rows.prompt: Describe what happens during puja.
rows.model_answer: Shoes are removed and women cover their heads; a bell is rung to begin. The image is dressed and garlanded, food is offered, and scripture is chanted while the devotee moves clockwise around the shrine. Water symbolises purity, incense is burned and a sacred lamp or fire burns.

rows.prompt: Describe how Hindus celebrate Divali.
rows.model_answer: Divali is a five-day autumn festival recalling the return of Rama and Sita from exile. Lamps and fireworks are lit, gifts exchanged and prayers offered to Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, who visits homes with a row of lights. Day four marks the New Year, a time for forgiving and good wishes; light symbolises the victory of goodness.

rows.prompt: Name two traditional practices outlawed in India and one Hindu influenced by Christian ideals.
rows.model_answer: Child marriage and sati or suttee, the burning of a widow beside her dead husband, are outlawed but hard to abolish, along with the treatment of Untouchables. Mahatma Gandhi (1869-1948), who lived passive resistance to British rule, was influenced by Christian ideals, as were Sri Ramakrishna and Rabindranath Tagore.

rows.prompt: Outline the Hindu vision of salvation, with reference to samsara, karma and moksha.
rows.model_answer: Hindus believe that a person is reborn many times until they become perfect. After death the soul, atman, moves into a new body, and this endless cycle of rebirth is called samsara. Where a person is reborn depends on karma, the law of cause and effect: do good and good will happen; do bad and bad will happen. Karma is not fatalistic, as through judgement and forethought it can be used to advantage. Hindus therefore try to follow their dharma, right conduct, showing virtues such as compassion, gentleness, modesty and forgiveness, as outlined in the Bhagavad Gita. This builds good karma and a better rebirth. Krishna says in the Gita that the spirit leaves the body like an old garment and puts on a new one, and 'you shall reap what you sow'. The goal is moksha, liberation from the cycle of rebirth and from ignorance, and complete union and peace with God. Spiritual perfection is when atman is at one with Brahman. The liberated soul rests in blissful isolation, by absorption into Brahman, or in communion with a personal god. Gurus in ashrams teach the way, and sadhus renounce earthly pleasures to reach it.

rows.prompt: Describe the Hindu caste system and discuss the challenge it presents to Hinduism today.
rows.model_answer: The caste system is an ancient social-class system in which people are born into groups, each with its own rules and traditions. Originally all classes were equal, but they came to be fixed by birth. Its origin is in the Rig-Veda: when Brahman's body was divided, his mouth became the priests, his arms the soldiers, his thighs the merchants and his feet the servants. So there are four varnas: Brahmins (teachers and priests), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers and merchants) and Shudras (labourers and servants). The Untouchables or Harijans are a separate non-caste group doing the lowliest jobs, such as working with leather. Today jobs no longer decide caste, but endogamy is the norm, and mixing brings penalties like ritual cleansing or paying for a feast. A person may move caste at rebirth after a good life. The challenge is human dignity. Louis Fischer called untouchability 'segregation gone mad'. Mahatma Gandhi fought it, defying 'a thousand taboos', and admitted untouchable families into his ashram and home. The treatment of Untouchables is outlawed by India's Assembly but is difficult to abolish.

rows.prompt: Describe two Hindu rites of passage and explain their significance.
rows.model_answer: At birth the family gathers and the father dips a gold pen in honey and writes the sacred syllable 'Aum' on the baby's tongue. The hope is that the child will grow to speak the truth, which is sweet like honey. Later the baby's first hair is cut, to show that badness from a previous life will not affect the new life - linking to belief in samsara and karma. Marriage is usually arranged and follows the Law of the Land, Customary Law and Brahmanical Law. The ceremony is in the bride's home; she wears a red sari and her hands and feet are painted with saffron. The marriage takes place around a sacred fire, symbol of the sun, with the god Agni as witness. The couple take seven steps around the fire representing food, wealth, strength, children, good luck, happiness and friendship. Guests pass their hands through the flame and touch their foreheads as cleansing. The groom gives a necklace of black beads and two gold semi-circles, showing the wedding unites two families.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 rites x 5 marks: description 3 marks + significance 2 marks. Credit: birth - Aum in honey, truth, hair cutting and previous life; Sacred Thread - Upanayana, twice born, puja; marriage - three laws, sacred fire, Agni, seven steps, necklace; death - cremation, male relative, ashes in river.

rows.prompt: Describe two Hindu festivals and explain the importance of festivals in Hinduism.
rows.model_answer: Hindu festivals are times of music, dance, stories and shared food. They break the daily routine and are times to celebrate and raise new hope. Hindus follow a lunar calendar, and the adventures of Rama, the seventh avatar of Vishnu, and his wife Sita feature in several festivals. Divali, meaning 'row of lights', is a five-day autumn festival recalling Rama and Sita's return from exile. Lamps and fireworks are lit, gifts exchanged and prayers offered to Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity, who visits every home that displays a row of lights. Day four marks the New Year, a time for forgiving and good wishes, and light symbolises the victory of goodness. Holi is a three-day festival of fertility with street dancing and bonfires. People sprinkle coloured powder and red-stained water to symbolise new blood in their veins. They worship statues of Krishna and his consort Radha, sing hymns, light candles in Arti services of light and share prasad, sacred food. Festivals also show that worship becomes congregational, with thousands attending.

rows.prompt: Discuss the challenges facing Hinduism in the modern world.
rows.model_answer: Millions of Hindus still practise as they have for centuries, but others, mostly in Western countries, try to do so within the demands of modern life. There are hundreds of sacred occasions involving fasting, bathing, chanting and offerings, and for many these are now combined into weekly temple visits and mantras and meditation at a home shrine. A second challenge is traditional practices such as child marriage, sati or suttee (burning a widow beside her dead husband) and the treatment of Untouchables. These are outlawed by India's Assembly but hard to abolish. Gandhi fought untouchability and admitted untouchable families into his home. A third challenge is inter-faith relations. Between the eleventh and eighteenth centuries Hindu-Muslim relations ranged from persecution to attempts to fuse both faiths, as under Akbar (1556-1605). Christianity arrived with the Portuguese in the sixteenth century, influencing Sri Ramakrishna, Rabindranath Tagore and Mahatma Gandhi. Yet most Indians are unaffected by missions, and there is growing resistance to conversion. Hindu teachers stress common links with other faiths, such as a Divine Power as source of life, the Golden Rule and the consequences of good and bad actions. The commercialising of yoga is also a challenge, losing its spiritual essence.
